extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, philosophy, and humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating conceptual criteria and empirical indicators used by psychologists and philosophers to define, explain, and test humor and laughter (e.g., conflict-mixture accounts, instinct theories, physiological accounts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-mixture definition (Hecker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hecker defined the comic as the simultaneous stimulation from one source of two feeling-qualities, pleasure and pain, of approximately equal strength, producing an oscillation of attention back and forth between these two feelings and having the character of an "intermittent joyful surprise."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hecker emphasizes "simultaneousness of the birth of the two feelings" as the 'point' of a joke; the oscillation between feelings is analogous to rapid alternation of light and dark. Criticisms: equal-strength assumption rules out the apparent surplus of pleasure the theory is meant to explain; the analogy to vision is frail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hecker's physiological mechanism for laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Hecker inferred from peripheral stimulation experiments (tickling) that stimulation of sympathetic nerves lowers blood-pressure in the brain, which innervates diaphragm muscles causing laughter; intermittent joyful surprise would intermittently stimulate sympathetic nerves and set in motion the same adjustive apparatus as tickling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hecker's physiology draws on animal experiments and observations like pupil dilation during tickling. The book notes this physiology "goes to pieces" because tickling is a peculiar peripheral stimulation and laughter follows only in certain moods and conditions, weakening the physiological account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kraepelin/Wundt unexpected-intellectual-contrast account
rubrics_metrics.description: Kraepelin (and Wundt following him) locate the comic in an "unexpected intellectual contrast" — separate ideas entering a totality of perception or thought are partly harmonious and partly contradictory, producing an oscillation of feelings in which the positive side (pleasure) prevails and is elevated through contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the official German-psychology deliverance on humor. The author treats the "oscillation of feelings" as an interesting myth and raises the unanswered question of why pleasure should be elevated rather than pain when both are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lipps: the comic is sui generis (uniqueness of humorous feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lipps's statement: "The feeling of the comic is a feeling of the comic and nothing else," asserting that the humorous emotion is unique and not reducible to other emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that humor meets the first of McDougall's tests for an instinct (unique, irreducible emotional quality). The author notes this helps separate the comic from feelings like reproach or gratitude, strengthening the claim that humor is a distinct emotional instinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: McDougall's three tests for instinctiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: McDougall's definition of an instinct and his proposed tests: (1) unique and irreducible quality of emotional excitement; (2) occurrence not only in man but also in higher animals; (3) occasional morbid exaggeration in otherwise sane healthy humans (hypertrophy or abnormal excitability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three criteria are presented as a framework to judge whether humor is an inherited instinct. The author evaluates humor against each test (claims novelty/uniqueness, discusses animal rudiments, and cites morbid laughter cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Early spontaneous appearance in children as evidence of instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous laughter appears early and spontaneously in children (we 'never have to teach children when to laugh; we have to teach them when not to laugh'), indicating that humor belongs among hereditary instincts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: babies' smiles and play-laughter; contrast between children's lustier laughter and adult refined humor; implication that instinctive laughter requires little instruction and is evidence for an inherited disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contagiousness/sympathy and suggestion as indicators of instinctive humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous laughter can be communicated by sympathy and by suggestion: seeing others laugh produces both laughter and humorous emotion even without knowing the cause; reputation or announcement of a comic event primes enjoyment (sense of humor is 'subject to stampede').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This communicability is used to refute purely mechanical or release theories of laughter; dependency on favorable atmosphere and suggestion is emphasized (e.g., a famed humorist's mere announcement creates readiness to enjoy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morbid exaggeration (rire hystérique, drug-induced comedy) as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of pathological or exaggerated humorous laughter (e.g., 'rire hysterique', perpetual laugh cases, and laughter induced by hashish) show the sense of humor can occur in morbidly intensified form, meeting McDougall's third test for an instinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: clinical cases of prolonged comedic mood, Binet and Raymond's case of a woman with four months of perpetual laugh; hashish inducing seizures of comic mood; author uses both pathological and non-pathological ecstatic comic fits as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative-animal evidence and behavioral caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations (Darwin, Romanes, others) that dogs and some monkeys exhibit laughter-like noises, motions, and playful responses suggest rudiments of a sense of the ludicrous in animals, but comparative psychology cautions against attributing human-like consciousness to animals and focuses on behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author concludes animal evidence neither proves nor opposes the instinct account but indicates rudimentary homologues exist in playful complex animals; emphasizes methodological caution in interpreting animal 'humor.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as an element of play and social welcome (function)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sense of humor is presented as a primary instinct functioning originally in the state of play and related to the gregarious instinct; smiling and laughing serve as social welcome signals and facilitate play and sociability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: laughter as social welcome has biological importance and explains many laughter-as-pleasure expressions; play-theory references (Groos, McDougall) and the claim that humor evolved as an equipment of complex organisms during infancy and play.

rubrics_metrics.name: General critique of conflict-mixture theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict-mixture theories (attributing joy to a mixture/contrast of pleasure and pain) fail to account for why the combination produces a surplus of pleasure rather than pain or mere cancellation; asserting 'pleasure prevails' is insufficient without explaining the mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author traces this unresolved question from Plato and earlier thinkers to nineteenth-century German psychology and concludes that what appears a pain-source in play is actually a source of pleasant emotional interest when attitude is playful (reframing apparent pain as ludicrous interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneousness ('point' of a joke) as crucial to comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Hecker (and Kraepelin) assert that the "simultaneousness of the birth of the two feelings" constitutes the so-called 'point' of a joke, and without this point the comic effect of a joke or anecdote is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion highlights temporal structure: the 'point' is the moment when contradictory ideas/feelings co-occur, producing the comic effect. The author acknowledges this as a nearer approach to the true 'point' of a joke despite other failings of the theory.
